notes.meaning: Saul did more than stand by. The word means he gladly approved of Stephen's killing. That same day the first great persecution of the whole church began, and believers fled into Judea and Samaria. Many commentators think 'all' means mainly the preachers, while the apostles bravely stayed to care for the flock.

Godly men gave Stephen a proper burial and wept loudly over him. They may have been devout Jews who were not yet open followers of Jesus. Either way, it was brave to honor a man the leaders had just put to death. They feared God more than persecution, and their grief shows how great a loss the church felt.

The word for 'destroy' pictures a wild animal tearing at its prey. Saul went from house to house hunting believers, and he did not spare women. Paul later looked back on this with deep shame (Acts 22:4; 26:10). It makes God's later grace to him all the more wonderful.

The persecution meant to stamp out the church ended up spreading it. Ordinary believers, not only leaders, told people about Jesus wherever they went. In this way they began to obey Jesus' command to be his witnesses in Judea and Samaria (Acts 1:8).

This Philip is not the apostle. He is one of the seven helpers chosen in Acts 6, later called 'the evangelist', a traveling preacher of the good news. Jews and Samaritans had long been bitter toward each other, yet Philip brought them the message. He 'proclaimed' Christ the way a herald announces a new king, to people already waiting for the Messiah, God's promised King (John 4:25).

The crowds listened to Philip with one mind. The miracles first caught their attention, and then helped them accept his message. The miracles were like God's seal, showing the message came from heaven.

Evil spirits left people with loud cries, showing they were being forced out by a stronger power. Many who were paralyzed or lame were healed. These healings also picture what the gospel does: it breaks Satan's hold and heals people who cannot help themselves.
The whole city was glad. Sick people were made well, and many came to know Christ. The gospel does not make people gloomy; it brings great joy wherever it is truly received.

Before Philip came, a man named Simon practiced magic arts, called sorcery, and amazed the people. He boasted that he was someone great. Everyone, from the poorest to the richest, called him 'the Great Power' of God, as if he were God's power in human form. Pride and the wish to seem great have always done much harm.
The people followed Simon because he had dazzled them for a long time. Old errors are hard to let go of. That makes their turning to Christ an even clearer sign of God's power.

When the people believed Philip's message about God's kingdom and about Jesus, they were baptized. Baptism is the washing with water that marks a person as joining Christ and his church. Both men and women were baptized, showing both are equally welcome in Christ. Now they saw and felt the real power of God, not Simon's tricks.

Even Simon believed and was baptized, and he stayed close to Philip. He was amazed because he knew his own wonders were fake, but Philip's were real. Being convinced the message was true is not the same as a changed heart. Philip could not see into Simon's heart, and the church must go by what people openly profess.

differ.view: Simon had a real but short-lived faith, somewhere between true faith and pretending, like seed that is choked before it ripens; it lacked denial of self.
His baptism brought no new birth, but if he later truly repented, its grace could become real without being baptized again.
Simon was never truly saved; real faith shows itself by repenting and keeping on, and outward Christian behavior does not prove conversion.

notes.meaning: When the apostles heard that Samaria had welcomed God's message, they sent Peter and John. They came to help Philip, approve his work, and bind the new believers to the church in Jerusalem. John had once wanted fire to fall on a Samaritan village (Luke 9:54); now he came to bless them. Peter was sent by the group, not giving the orders himself.

Peter and John prayed that the new believers would receive the Holy Spirit. Older commentators take this as the special, visible gifts first given at Pentecost. We too can pray for God's Spirit to work in our children, friends, and pastors.

The Spirit had not yet 'fallen' on them in the special, outward way seen at Pentecost. Many traditional commentators say they already had the Spirit's saving work, since no one believes without him. 'Only baptized' does not belittle baptism. It means they had not yet received extra gifts, such as speaking in other languages.

differ.view: Many see a pattern here: believers are converted first and may receive the Holy Spirit in a later experience.
The Samaritans already had the Spirit who makes us God's children; what came now were special gifts given only for a time in the church's early days.
God held back the Spirit this one time so the Samaritan and Jerusalem believers would know they were one church; it is not a pattern for today.

notes.meaning: Peter and John placed their hands on the believers, and they received the Holy Spirit. Laying on of hands was a sign that went with prayer. The gift came from God, not from the apostles themselves; they were only his instruments.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: The Catholic rite of confirmation looks to this passage, where the Spirit is given through prayer and the laying on of hands.

notes.meaning: Simon saw something happen that could be seen, such as people speaking in new languages. He offered money for the power to give the Spirit to others. He did not ask to receive the Spirit himself; he wanted honor and profit. From his name we get 'simony', the buying and selling of church positions or holy things.

Peter flatly refused. His words mean, 'Your money go to destruction with you!' It was a stern warning that Simon was headed for ruin, not a final curse, since Peter goes on to urge him to repent. God's gifts are free and can never be bought.

Simon had no share at all in this work or in God's grace. His heart was not right with God; he loved money and fame more than Christ. Peter could judge this from this one act, because it showed what was really driving him.

Even after such a sharp rebuke, Peter did not shut the door. He told Simon to repent, which means to turn away from his sin with sorrow, and to pray. The 'perhaps' was doubt about whether Simon would truly repent, not about whether God would forgive him if he did.

'Poisoned by bitterness' pictures sin as a bitter, deadly poison filling his heart. 'Captive to iniquity' means sin held him like a chained prisoner. Peter saw that Simon's problem was not one slip but a heart still ruled by sin.

Simon was frightened and asked the apostles to pray for him. But he did not pray for himself, and he seemed more afraid of punishment than sorry for his sin. Scripture says nothing more about him. Later stories about him are full of legend and cannot be trusted.
Peter and John confirmed what Philip had taught and preached God's word in the city. On the way home they preached in many Samaritan villages. Small places have souls just as precious as big cities.

An angel told Philip to leave a busy, fruitful work and go to a lonely desert road toward Gaza. He was not told why. God sometimes opens doors in very unlikely places, and he asks us to obey even when we cannot see the reason.

Philip met an important official from Ethiopia in Africa, south of Egypt. He was in charge of the treasury of the queen, whose royal title was 'Candace'. 'Eunuch' was often a title for high court officials. He had traveled far to worship the God of Israel and was now reading Isaiah aloud in his chariot, making good use of his travel time.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some read him as a literal eunuch and see the story showing that people with all kinds of bodies were welcome in the early church. The servant's humiliation and lack of descendants in Isaiah may have matched his own situation.

notes.meaning: Now the Holy Spirit spoke to Philip, perhaps as a clear inner voice. He told Philip to go right up to the chariot. At last Philip began to see why God had sent him there.

Philip ran, eager to obey. He heard the man reading aloud and asked a simple question about whether he understood. He did not start with small talk about the weather or news, but went straight to what mattered most.

This powerful man humbly admitted he needed help and invited a stranger on foot to sit with him. To understand the Bible we need guides: good teachers, good books, and above all God's Spirit. God sent a man, not an angel, showing he uses human teachers to explain his word.

He was reading Isaiah 53:7-8 in its Greek version. It pictures someone led to death like a silent lamb, which fits Jesus' patient, willing suffering. He was denied justice and his life was taken. The line about his 'descendants' is read as his endless life after rising, or as the countless spiritual children his death would bring.

His question was natural, because the passage does not name the person. It shows he had thought hard about it. Ancient Jewish teachers had applied this passage to the Messiah. Good questions open the way to good teaching.

Philip used this very passage as his starting point and told him the good news about Jesus. He showed that Jesus fits Isaiah's picture and fulfills the Old Testament. When Christ is made known, we have the heart of the gospel.

Philip must have explained baptism as part of following Jesus. When they came to water, the man was eager not to delay. He humbly asked if anything stood in the way. Giving ourselves to God is best done without putting it off.

Philip said that faith from the whole heart was needed, and the man confessed that Jesus Christ is the Son of God. His confession is short but covers what matters: Jesus is the promised Messiah and God's Son. Most commentators note this verse is missing from the oldest copies of Acts and was probably added early. Still, what it says is taught throughout Scripture.

differ.view: Some argue the verse should be kept, because it records a genuine early confession of faith.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: The verse is seen as a very old addition shaped by the baptism service. It teaches that adults need faith before baptism, while infants are baptized in the faith of the Church.

notes.meaning: The official ordered the chariot to stop. Both men went down into the water, and Philip baptized him. Philip did not hold back, even though Simon had recently fooled him; the door into the church should be no narrower than Christ made it.

differ.view: New Testament baptism was by immersion, putting the whole person under the water.
The text does not prove immersion; the early church may have immersed, but the way water is applied is not essential, and sprinkling is also valid.
Methodist commentators differ: one says 'went down' just means leaving the chariot and the text says nothing about the method; another thinks he went under the water.

notes.meaning: As they came out of the water, the Spirit suddenly and miraculously took Philip away, as happened to some Old Testament prophets. The man went on his way full of joy. His faith rested on God, not on Philip. Tradition says he later preached in Ethiopia, though that is not certain.

differ.view: Some think this was not a miracle of movement, but the Spirit strongly urging Philip to leave quickly for other work.

notes.meaning: Philip next appeared at Azotus, the Old Testament town of Ashdod, near the coast. He did not sit idle but preached in every town until he reached Caesarea. He later made his home there (Acts 21:8).

problems: v. 16: dropped differ point (Methodist): no checkable source
v. 37: dropped differ point (Reformed and Presbyterian): no checkable source
